title: the lac house
hook: the city mourns the living, and in the forest Bhima keeps watch

segments.voice: Yesterday: nauka, the boat at the Ganga, its boatman proved by Vidura's own words. Your line was quiet help, hidden in plain sight.

In Hastinapura, the news arrives: the Pandavas are dead, burned at Varanavata with their mother. Dhritarashtra weeps, the text says, and orders the rites for the dead. Water is offered for them. The people mourn. Vidura grieves only a little, because he knows. Far away, the five brothers and their mother are alive, asleep on the ground. Two places, and two kinds of grief.

In the forest they've gone as far as they can. Kunti is exhausted and thirsty. Bhima goes for water, and by the time he's back they're all asleep on the bare ground under a tree. So Bhima sits up alone and looks at them. The text gives him a lament here. In paraphrase: what could hurt more than this, my brothers sleeping on the earth, my mother lying in the open. He thinks of Duryodhana, and his anger rises. He could go back and end it, he says. But Yudhishthira isn't angry, and Bhima won't move without him. So he stays, and keeps watch. Set the two scenes side by side. In the city, a king weeps for nephews his own son tried to kill, and the text doesn't tell us how to weigh those tears. Vidura holds his secret and says little. In the forest, the brother known for his strength, and for his anger, spends it sitting still. Bhima is the brother we first met shaking boys out of a tree. Here, at the end of the lac house, his strength takes another shape: he stays awake so the others can rest. The house is ash. The family is homeless, mourned as dead, sleeping in the open. And one of them watches over the rest.
screen: `ASLEEP ON THE BARE GROUND.` · `BHIMA'S LAMENT, AND HIS ANGER.` · `HE WON'T MOVE WITHOUT YUDHISHTHIRA.` · then, large: `STRENGTH THAT KEEPS WATCH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who'll be asleep tonight, under your roof, in your city or far away; if you live alone, think of one person, wherever they are. See them resting, and for a moment be the one awake, like Bhima under the tree. There's nothing to do for them; just keep watch in your mind, breathing slowly, while they sleep.
Bhima, the brother known for strength and anger, who spends this night sitting still, keeping watch while his family sleeps.
Your line: strength that keeps watch. Bhima's anger found another shape. Day seven hundred thirty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Offering water for the dead, called tarpana, is part of Hindu funeral and remembrance rites; in this story the offering is made for the Pandavas while they are still alive.

fork.setup: you're Bhima. your family is asleep on the ground, and the man who tried to burn them is in a palace. what do you do?
options: go back tonight and settle it.
wake Yudhishthira and argue for revenge.
stay where you are, and keep watch.
fork.reveal: he stays. his anger is real, the text says, but Yudhishthira isn't angry, so Bhima keeps watch while the others sleep.

original.note: Sanskrit bhīma: terrible, formidable; the name of the brother known for strength, who here uses his strength to sit still.

chat.says: Bhima's the strong, angry one, right? Why didn't he go back and fight Duryodhana?
options: He wouldn't act without Yudhishthira, so he stayed and kept watch while they slept.
He was too worn out from carrying everyone, so he fell asleep with them.
Kunti made him promise never to fight his cousins, so he let it go.
chat.meaning: Bhima's anger rose, but Yudhishthira wasn't angry, and Bhima wouldn't move without him. So he spent his strength keeping watch.

Hastinapura.meaning: the Kuru capital, where the court mourns the Pandavas

Dhritarashtra.meaning: the blind king, uncle of the Pandavas

Duryodhana.meaning: Dhritarashtra's eldest son, the Pandavas' rival cousin

Varanavata.meaning: the town where the house of lac burned

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha Parva (the mourning at Hastinapura; Dhritarashtra's grief and the water rites; Vidura grieves little)
Mahabharata, Adi Parva, opening of Hidimba-vadha Parva (Bhima fetches water and keeps watch; his lament over his sleeping family)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Dhritarashtra weeps and orders the funeral and water rites; Vidura grieves little because he knows.
Bhima's lament and his line that he would act but for Yudhishthira's lack of anger are paraphrased from the opening of the Hidimba-vadha section; confirm wording and placement.

Hidimba, Ghatotkacha, Ekachakra and Baka fall between this day and the swayamvara in the text; the outline passes over them, so this script ends the lac house before Hidimba arrives. A Keeper may want them named in passing.
The readings of Dhritarashtra's tears were cut in the editor pass (see below).
